texts.preamble: In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 In The Court Of Sh. Ashu Garg, Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate - Ii (New Delhi), Patiala House Courts, New Delhi Cc No. 123/04 Unique Case Id No. 02403R0906232004 Date of Institution: 29.06.2004 Date of reserving judgement: 28.11.2016 Date of pronouncement: 05.12.2016 In re: Delhi Administration / Food Inspector Department of Pfa, Govt. of Nct of Delhi A-20, Lawrence Road Industrial Area, Delhi-110035 ... texts.facts: The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (Pfa Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of the Pfa Act and Rules. The acc used mani Ram is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. Aggarwal Sweet India, from where the food article, that is, 'Boondi Laddu' was lifted for sampling. 2. As per the complaint, on 28.02.2004, food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Sanjeev Kumar Gupta and Food Assistant (FA) Brahma Nand under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Harish Kumar Ahuja reached along with their staff at the premises in question where the accused was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption. The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Boondi Laddu from the vendor lying in an open tray (ready for sale) bearing no label declaration, to which he agreed. The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules. Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama, etc. The price of sample was paid to the vendor. Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA. Vide report dated 12.03.2004, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that the total dye content of synthetic colour used exceeded the prescribed maximum In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/ 1 limit'. Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI. After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA. The complaint was then filed in the court by FI on 29.06.2004 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(j) and (m) of PFA Act as well as Rules 28, 29 and 30 of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act. 3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 29.06.2004. Upon appearance, the accused moved an application thereby exercising his right under section 13(2) PFA Act to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed by the Central Food Laboratory (CFL). However, the accused made statement on 16.08.2005 that he was not inclined to send the sample for analysis to CFL and wanted to withdraw his application. The said application was thus dismissed as withdrawn. 4. The matter was then listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 FI Sanjeev Kumar. On the basis of his deposition, charge was framed against the accused on 01.09.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a), (j) and (m) of PFA Act, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. At the trial, the witness already examined in pre-charge stage was recalled for further cross-examination in post-charge stage and additionally, the prosecution examined PW-2 Sh. Harish Kumar Ahuja (SDM/LHA) and PW-3 FA Brahmanand in post- charge stage. 5. At the trial, PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 who were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings, deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 28.02.2004 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 1500 gms of Boondi Laddu taken from an open tray, payment of price of sample, breaking the commodity into smallest possible pieces using a clean and dry steel spoon, mixing it using the said spoon, dividing them by putting them equally in three clean and dry sample glass bottles, adding 40 drops of formalin as preservative, separately sealing, packing and marking the sample bottles and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses. They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, Notice as per Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B and Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C. On the next working day, that is 01.03.2004, one counterpart of sample along with Memo as per Form-VII were sent to PA for analysis vide PA Receipt Ex. PW-1 /D and remaining two counterparts with copy of Memos were deposited with LHA/SDM vide receipt Ex. PW-1/E. PA report Ex. PW-1/F was received and upon direction of SDM/LHA, investigation was carried out by PW-1. He sent letter Ex. PW-1/G to the STO and received its reply. He also received reply Ex. PW-1/H from the accused. After completion of the investigation, sanction/consent Ex. PW-1/J was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/K was filed in the court. After this, intimation letter Ex. PW-1/L with copy of PA report was sent to the accused through registered post vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/M and was also personally delivered to the accused against proper endorsement. These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence counsel wherein they denied that the sample proceedings were not proper or that the accused had been falsely implicated. In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/ 2 6. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 23.03.2016 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence. He accepted the proceedings dated 28.02.2004, though claimed that sampling method was not proper and the sample bottles were not cleaned despite his request. He however did not lead any evidence in defence.
texts.arguments: 7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that he has not been able to rebut the findings in the PA report dated 12.03.2004. It is pointed out that the accused has failed to exercise his right under section 13(2) PFA Act and failed to get the sample analysed from CFL. It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony. 8. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various missing links in the testimony of witnesses. Ld. Counsel as questioned the PA report on the ground that there has been an unexplained delay of three days in signing the report, relying upon the judgements titled as Delhi Administration v. Amar Chand [2012 (3) JCC 1930] and State of Gujrat v. Vishramdas Virumal [2005 (1) FAC 48]. It is further submitted that Tartrazine is not a harmful colouring matter as its use is permitted in many food articles. Ld. Counsel has also submitted that there were violations of various provisions of PFA Rules during sample proceedings in as much as the spoon and sample bottles used were not made clean and dry, and also that no independent public witness was joined in the proceedings. It is finally contended that the laboratory in which the sample was analysed and the testing method were not notified under the Rules and therefore the prosecution is bad in law. Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone, if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies. No such In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/ 5 inconsistency can be seen in this case. Relying upon the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Food Inspector [2010(2) PFA Cases 310], Defence counsel has argued that the prosecution was bad in law and no prosecution could have been launched because Section 23, which empowered the Central Government to make rules to carry out the provisions of the Act, was amended with effect from 01.04.1976 and Sub Clause (ee) and (hh) were inserted in Clause (1A) of section 23 which included power to define/ designate laboratories competent to analyze the sample as well as define the methods of analysis to be used. The relevant portion of the judgement relied upon by the Ld. Defence counsel reads as: "34. Consequently, the High Court also erred in holding that the non- formulation of Rules under the aforesaid provisions of the 1954 Act could not be said In Re vs Mani Ram on 5 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/144865504/ 8 to be fatal for the prosecution." The present case would be squarely covered by the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Prem Ballab v. State (Delhi Administration) [(1977) 1 SCC 173]. This judgement was discussed even in Pepsico's case, but was never disturbed and was sought to be distinguished on the ground that this was dealing with colouring matter (as in the present case) and not with pesticides in carbonated water. The judgements titled as Mangal Singh v. State [1976(II) PFA Cases 139], Hans Raj v. State of Punjab [1980(II) PFA Cases 396], State of Himachal Pradesh v. Kamlesh Chand [2002(2) FAC 315], State of Orrisa v. Rabindra Sahu [2006(1) FAC 200], State of MP v. Uma Shankar [2007 FAJ 478], State of Maharashtra v. Raj Karan [1988(II) PFA Cases 156], Delhi Administration v. Suraj [Crl. A No. 192/2005, Delhi High Court, dated 10.12.2013] would apply to their own set of facts, circumstances and evidence where it was found that some rule was not complied with. But in this case, the evidence is not disclosing non-compliance of any rule. Similarly, judgements titled as Shew Chand Mathur v. State of Assam [1991(1) PFA Cases 9] and State of Gujarat v. Laghadhirbhai Vaghjibhai Prajapati [2009(2) CCC 134] deal with non-compliance of Rule 14, but in this case, there is positive corroborative evidence to show compliance of such provisions. Similar observation applies to judgements titled as State v. Banwari Lal [2011(1) FAC 149] and Gian Chand v. State of Haryana [1982(I) PFA Cases 8] that pertain to rule 18.
